newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's UDF nominates reformist Kostov as PM.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's UDF nominates reformist Kostov as PM.

text.p: Bulgaria's Union of Democratic Forces on Thursday nominated its leader Ivan Kostov as prime minister to implement belated market reforms and bring the country out of crisis.

His nomination must be approved by the new parliament, and Kostov proposed to President Petar Stoyanov that he should convene its first session on May 7. Bulgaria has four days' holiday next week for Orthodox Easter and Labour Day.
Stoyanov must then ask Kostov formally to form a cabinet, which Kostov said would be ready on about May 20.
"The future Bulgarian cabinet will rely on the reformist majority in society which is expected to support its reforms and to save Bulgaria," Kostov told a news conference.

Results of Saturday's elections showed the UDF and its coalition allies won 52 percent of the vote and 137 seats in the 240-seat parliament, compared to 22 percent and 58 seats for the former ruling Socialists. Three smaller parties will also be represented.
The 47-year-old coalition leader has said he wants the new parliament to vote a declaration agreeing on the basic principles for finding a way out of the crisis.
It must also pass a 1997 budget and a package of laws to permit introduction of a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime agreed with the International Monetary Fund.

"A top priority of the UDF is the financial and economic stabilisation of the country and this is why the law for introduction of a currency board system and the state budget are going to be the first passed by the parliament," said Ekaterina Mihailova, chairwoman of the UDF parliamentary group.

She said these laws and about another 10 urgent economic measures should be passed by the parliament within 30 days of its taking office, and then the UDF would propose laws for fighting organised crime and corruption.

Bulgaria's legal system needs updating to deal with an explosion of crime since the end of one-party rule in 1989. The interior ministry is preparing new laws to criminalise racketeering and tax evasion.

Kostov said he expected to retain some ministers from the interim cabinet. "It is no secret that the current interior minister Bogomil Bonev is our favourite for the same ministry and (deputy premier) Alexander Bozhkov will be the 'live link' between the two cabinets," he said.
The UDF will nominate the former chairman of the UDF parliamentary group, Yordan Sokolov, for parliamentary speaker.
Kostov, a former finance minister, was a central figure in month-long protests which toppled the Socialists in February and forced the holding of elections nearly two years early.
He has a tough act to follow in interim prime minister Stefan Sofianski, Sofia's popular UDF mayor, who has led a succesful caretaker cabinet since the Socialists stepped down.
Monthly inflation has slowed to four to five percent in April from 12 percent in March and 243 percent in February and the lev currency has stabilised.
An associate professor of economics, Kostov has served twice as finance minister -- once in a 1990 caretaker government and then in 1991.

The National Statistics Institute said on Thursday the collapse of the lev in 1996, shrinking demand, a drastic fall in purchasing power and delayed structural reform had made Bulgaria a laggard among former East Bloc economies last year.
It said 1996 Gross Domestic Product fell by a real 10.9 percent compared to 2.5 percent growth in 1995.
